mainTopic: God's prayer, God's moment of anger and בלעם, משה's requests from God, and God's promises of good
overview: This amud is a chain of אגדות, many of them from רבי יוחנן in the name of רבי יוסי. It opens with the idea that הקדוש ברוך הוא 'prays' that His mercy will overcome His anger. רבי ישמעאל בן אלישע blesses God with those same words in the קודש הקדשים, which teaches that we should never take an ordinary person's ברכה lightly. Next comes the lesson not to appease someone while he is still angry. This leads to a discussion of God's anger: it is real but lasts only a רגע, and only בלעם knew how to pinpoint that moment. God's kindness was that He did not become angry at all in בלעם's days. The גמרא gives the timing and sign of that moment, the rooster, and tells how רבי יהושע בן לוי learned that it is wrong to use it to curse anyone. After a teaching that inner regret is worth more than many lashes, the גמרא turns to משה's three requests from God. Among them is the question of why צדיקים suffer and רשעים prosper, followed by teachings on משה seeing God's 'back.' The amud ends by proving from משה's descendants that God never takes back a promise of good.

steps.title: God prays: the proof from a פסוק in ישעיה
steps.stepSummary: רבי יוחנן, quoting רבי יוסי, proves from the words 'בית תפלתי' ('My house of prayer') that הקדוש ברוך הוא Himself prays.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי יוחנן said in the name of רבי יוסי: How do we know that הקדוש ברוך הוא prays? Because the פסוק says, 'I will bring them to My holy mountain and make them joyful in the house of My prayer.' It does not say 'their prayer.' It says 'My prayer.' From here we learn that הקדוש ברוך הוא prays.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא presents a surprising statement: God Himself prays. It backs this up with an exact reading of one word in a פסוק.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The פסוק could simply have called the בית המקדש the house of 'their' prayer, meaning the people's prayer. Because the פסוק chose the word 'תפלתי' (My prayer), רבי יוסי reads it as describing a prayer that belongs to God Himself. The proof works through a precise word-choice דיוק.

keyTerms.meaning: From where do we know? (asks for a source)
It does not say X, but rather Y (a precise word-choice inference)

steps.confusionAlert: Do not picture God asking a higher power for something. As the next steps show, God's 'prayer' is an expression of His own will: that His mercy should win out over strict judgment.

phrases.aramaic: אָמַר רַבִּי יוֹחָנָן מִשּׁוּם רַבִּי יוֹסֵי:
phrases.english: Rabbi Yochanan said in the name of Rabbi Yosei:
From where do we know that the Holy One, Blessed be He, prays?
As it says: 'I will bring them to My holy mountain
and make them joyful in the house of My prayer'
phrases.notes: ישעיה נו:ז

phrases.english: It does not say 'their prayer,' but rather 'My prayer.'
From here we learn that the Holy One, Blessed be He, prays.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Opens this passage (in context, it continues the daf's theme of describing God in human-like terms).
steps.mimraCoreRuling: הקדוש ברוך הוא prays, as shown by the word 'תפלתי' in ישעיה נו:ז.

steps.title: What does God pray?
steps.stepSummary: Once we know God prays, the גמרא asks what the content of that prayer is.
steps.simpleTranslation: What does He pray?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks a short follow-up question. It is setting up the next step, which will give the actual words of God's prayer.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Step 1 told us only that God prays. This question is not an attack on that idea. It asks for missing information: what such a prayer could possibly say.

phrases.english: What does He pray?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Follows up on step 1 by asking for the content of God's prayer.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: The actual words or content of God's prayer.

steps.title: God's prayer: that mercy should overcome anger
steps.stepSummary: רב, quoted by רב זוטרא בר טוביה, gives God's prayer: that His רחמים should overcome His anger and that He should treat His children לפנים משורת הדין.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב זוטרא בר טוביה said in the name of רב: God prays, 'May it be My will that My mercy overcomes My anger, that My mercy prevails over My other attributes, that I treat My children with the attribute of mercy, and that I go beyond the letter of the law for them.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the question by quoting God's prayer in four short lines. Every line is about mercy winning over strict judgment.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The prayer is addressed 'מלפני', from before Myself. So it is God's own wish, not a request to someone else. Strict judgment (מדת הדין) may call for punishment, and God 'prays' that His love for His children will lead Him to act with more kindness than the law strictly demands.

keyTerms.meaning: May it be My will (literally: 'from before Me')
And they will prevail or 'roll over'
Beyond the strict letter of the law

steps.whyThisMatters: This text is the source for the idea that God Himself 'desires' to act with רחמים, and it becomes the model for the ברכה in the next story.

phrases.aramaic: אָמַר רַב זוּטְרָא בַּר טוֹבִיָּה, אָמַר רַב:
phrases.english: Rav Zutra bar Toviah said in the name of Rav:
'May it be My will
that My mercy overcomes My anger,
and that My mercy prevails over My other attributes,
and that I act toward My children with the attribute of mercy,
and that I go beyond the letter of the law for them.'

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַב זוּטְרָא בַּר טוֹבִיָּה, אָמַר רַב
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question asked in step 2.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: God prays that His mercy should overcome His anger and His other attributes, and that He should deal with His children with mercy, beyond the letter of the law.

steps.title: רבי ישמעאל blesses God in the קודש הקדשים
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא tells how רבי ישמעאל בן אלישע, the כהן גדול, saw a vision of God in the קודש הקדשים. God asked him for a ברכה, and he blessed God with the very words of God's own prayer. God nodded in acceptance.
steps.simpleTranslation: It was taught in a ברייתא: רבי ישמעאל בן אלישע said, 'Once I entered the innermost chamber to offer קטורת. I saw אכתריאל יה ה' צבאות sitting on a high and lofty throne. He said to me, 'ישמעאל, My son, bless Me!' I said to Him: 'May it be Your will that Your mercy overcomes Your anger, that Your mercy prevails over Your other attributes, that You act toward Your children with the attribute of mercy, and that You go beyond the letter of the law for them.' And He nodded His head to me.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a story from a ברייתא that matches רב's words. A person blesses God using exactly the prayer that God Himself prays.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ברכה רבי ישמעאל gives is word-for-word the prayer from step 3, changed from 'My' to 'Your'. This supports the idea that God desires this kind of prayer. God's nod shows that He accepted the ברכה.

keyTerms.meaning: It was taught in a ברייתא
The innermost place: the קודש הקדשים
A name of God expressing His crown or authority
And He nodded His head to me

steps.confusionAlert: Notice that רבי ישמעאל does not invent a new blessing. He repeats God's own prayer from step 3, simply turned from first person into second person.

phrases.aramaic: תַּנְיָא, אָמַר רַבִּי יִשְׁמָעֵאל בֶּן אֱלִישָׁע:
phrases.english: It was taught: Rabbi Yishmael ben Elisha said:
Once, I entered to offer the incense
in the innermost chamber (the Holy of Holies),
phrases.notes: On יום כפור, the only time the כהן גדול entered

phrases.english: and I saw Akatriel Yah, the Lord of Hosts,

phrases.aramaic: שֶׁהוּא יוֹשֵׁב עַל כִּסֵּא רָם וְנִשָּׂא,
phrases.english: sitting on a high and lofty throne,
and He said to me: 'Yishmael, My son, bless Me!'
I said to Him: 'May it be Your will
that Your mercy overcomes Your anger,
and that Your mercy prevails over Your other attributes,
and that You act toward Your children with the attribute of mercy,
and that You go beyond the letter of the law for them.'
And He nodded His head to me.

steps.triggerLanguage: תַּנְיָא, אָמַר רַבִּי יִשְׁמָעֵאל בֶּן אֱלִישָׁע
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Brings a ברייתא story whose blessing matches the content of God's prayer given in step 3.
steps.raayaObject: The idea that God's desired 'prayer' is for His mercy to overcome His anger.
steps.raayaSupportSource: A ברייתא recounting רבי ישמעאל בן אלישע's vision in the קודש הקדשים.

steps.title: Lesson: never take an ordinary person's blessing lightly
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא draws a practical lesson from the story: we should value even a simple person's ברכה.
steps.simpleTranslation: And this teaches us that the blessing of an ordinary person should not be taken lightly in your eyes.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא tells us the point of the story. If God asked for a human's ברכה and accepted it, we should certainly value the ברכה of any person.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The phrase 'וקא משמע לן' signals the lesson the story comes to teach. The reasoning is a קל וחומר: if God Himself valued a ברכה from a human being, then a person must surely value a ברכה from another person, even a הדיוט.

keyTerms.meaning: The blessing of an ordinary (non-distinguished) person

steps.whatToRemember: God 'prays' that His mercy will overcome His anger and that He will treat us לפנים משורת הדין. When רבי ישמעאל blessed God with these words, God accepted them. The lesson: never take any person's ברכה lightly.
steps.whyThisMatters: This is a well-known source for valuing ברכות from anyone, not only from גדולים.

phrases.english: And this teaches us
that the blessing of an ordinary person should not be
light in your eyes.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Draws the practical lesson from the story in step 4.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: One should not take lightly the blessing of an ordinary person, since God Himself requested and accepted a human being's blessing.

steps.title: Don't try to calm someone while they are still angry
steps.stepSummary: רבי יוחנן, in the name of רבי יוסי, learns from the פסוק 'פני ילכו והנחתי לך' that you should not try to appease a person at the height of his anger. God told משה to wait until His 'face of anger' passed.
steps.simpleTranslation: And רבי יוחנן said in the name of רבי יוסי: How do we know that you should not try to calm a person down while he is still angry? Because it says 'My face will go, and I will give you rest.' God said to משה: Wait for Me until My angry face passes, and then I will give you what you asked for.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי יוחנן gives a new teaching about good behavior: wait for someone's anger to pass before you try to make peace. He brings a פסוק as the source.
steps.deeperAnalysis: After the חטא העגל, משה asked God to bring the שכינה back to the Jewish people. רבי יוחנן reads 'פני ילכו' as 'My angry face will go away first', and 'והנחתי לך' as 'then I will grant your request.' If God Himself asked משה to wait, then we too should wait for a person to calm down before trying to appease him.

keyTerms.meaning: appease, try to calm someone down
at the time of his anger, while he is still angry
'My face will go' (read here as: My angry face will pass)

steps.whyThisMatters: This is a practical lesson in בין אדם לחבירו. Trying to make peace too early can make things worse. It also opens the topic of God's anger, which the rest of this passage explores.

phrases.aramaic: וְאָמַר רַבִּי יוֹחָנָן מִשּׁוּם רַבִּי יוֹסֵי:
phrases.english: And Rabbi Yochanan said in the name of Rabbi Yosei:
phrases.notes: The same chain of tradition as the earlier teaching that God prays.

phrases.english: From where do we know that we do not appease a person
at the time of his anger?
As it is written: 'My face will go, and I will give you rest' (Shemos 33:14).
phrases.notes: Said after the חטא העגל, in reply to משה's request.

phrases.aramaic: אָמַר לוֹ הַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא לְמֹשֶׁה:
phrases.english: The Holy One, Blessed be He, said to Moshe:

phrases.aramaic: הַמְתֵּן לִי עַד שֶׁיַּעַבְרוּ פָּנִים שֶׁל זַעַם
phrases.english: Wait for Me until the face of anger passes,
and then I will grant you your request.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְאָמַר רַבִּי יוֹחָנָן מִשּׁוּם רַבִּי יוֹסֵי: מִנַּיִן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: A new teaching in the same series of statements from רבי יוחנן in the name of רבי יוסי. It still deals with how God relates to His people.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: One should not try to appease a person while he is still angry. Wait until the anger passes, as God told משה to wait.

steps.title: Can God really be described as angry?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא questions the idea behind רבי יוחנן's reading. Is there really such a thing as anger before הקדוש ברוך הוא?
steps.simpleTranslation: But is there really anger before the Holy One, Blessed be He?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא pushes back on the idea that God has a 'face of anger' at all. It is asking whether this is even a proper way to speak about God.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי יוחנן's derivation only works if God actually gets angry and then calms down. The גמרא checks this assumption, since describing God as 'angry' seems hard to accept. If there were no such thing, the proof from the פסוק would fall apart.

keyTerms.meaning: but is there really...? (a challenging question)
before the Holy One, Blessed be He

phrases.english: But is there anger
before the Holy One, Blessed be He?

steps.triggerLanguage: וּמִי אִיכָּא רִתְחָא קַמֵּיהּ דְּקוּדְשָׁא בְּרִיךְ הוּא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the hidden assumption in step 6 that God has 'a face of anger.'
steps.kashyaTarget: The assumption in step 6 that God gets angry.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: It seems wrong to say that God gets angry. If He doesn't, then 'פנים של זעם' cannot mean God's anger, and the proof for the practical rule fails.

steps.title: Yes, a ברייתא says God is angry every day
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers yes, God does have anger. A ברייתא quotes the פסוק 'ואל זועם בכל יום', 'God is angry every day.'
steps.simpleTranslation: Yes, as it was taught in a ברייתא: 'And God is angry every day.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers its own question. A ברייתא based on a פסוק in תהלים shows that God does have anger.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The פסוק in תהלים (7:12) states clearly that God is 'זועם' (angry) every day. So speaking of God's anger is a real תורה concept, not something invented. רבי יוחנן's reading in step 6 stands.

keyTerms.meaning: as it was taught in a ברייתא

phrases.english: Yes,
as it was taught: 'And God is angry every day' (Tehillim 7:12).

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of step 7 directly.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Proof from a ברייתא quoting a פסוק
steps.terutzHavaAmina: We might have thought it is improper to say God gets angry.
steps.terutzMaskana: A פסוק explicitly says God is angry every day, so God's anger is a real concept.

steps.title: God's anger lasts only one tiny moment
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא continues: God's anger lasts only a רגע, a moment. A רגע is one part out of 58,888 parts of an hour.
steps.simpleTranslation: How long does His anger last? A moment. And how long is a moment? One part out of 58,888 of an hour. That is a moment.
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא now measures how long God's daily anger lasts. It gives an exact, extremely short length of time.
steps.deeperAnalysis: 'בכל יום' could sound like God is angry for long stretches. The ברייתא limits it to a single רגע, a tiny fraction of an hour (רבוא means 10,000, so 5 רבוא + 8,000 + 888 = 58,888). This shows that God's anger is real but extremely brief.

keyTerms.meaning: a moment, a set tiny unit of time

steps.confusionAlert: This is still part of the ברייתא, not a new question from the גמרא. The ברייתא asks and answers its own questions ('וכמה... וכמה...') to describe the length of God's anger.

phrases.english: And how long is His anger? A moment.
And how long is a moment?
One part out of fifty thousand and eight thousand,
and eight hundred eighty-eight, of an hour,
phrases.notes: Total: 1/58,888 of an hour.

phrases.english: and that is a moment.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the same ברייתא and defines how long the anger mentioned in step 8 lasts.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: God's anger lasts only one רגע, which is 1/58,888 of an hour.

steps.title: Only בלעם could pinpoint that moment
steps.stepSummary: No creature can identify the exact moment of God's anger except בלעם הרשע, about whom it says 'ויודע דעת עליון'.
steps.simpleTranslation: And no creature can pinpoint that exact moment, except for בלעם the wicked, about whom it is written: 'and he knows the knowledge of the Most High.'
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא adds that the moment of God's anger is hidden from everyone except בלעם. This sets up the next discussion on the daf about בלעם and that moment.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Since the moment is so tiny, nobody can time it, with one exception. The פסוק calls בלעם 'יודע דעת עליון', one who knows the knowledge of the Most High. The גמרא reads this as knowing exactly when God's anger strikes, which explains how בלעם hoped to curse the Jewish people.

keyTerms.meaning: to pinpoint, to aim at precisely
בלעם the wicked, the prophet hired to curse the Jewish people
'and he knows the knowledge of the Most High' (במדבר כד:טז)

steps.whatToRemember: God's anger is real but lasts only one tiny רגע. Only בלעם knew how to pinpoint it. Just as God told משה to wait for His anger to pass, we should wait for a person's anger to pass before trying to make peace.

phrases.english: And no creature is able
to pinpoint that moment,
except for Bilaam the wicked,
as it is written about him: 'and he knows the knowledge of the Most High' (Bamidbar 24:16).

steps.triggerLanguage: וְאֵין כָּל בְּרִיָּה יְכוֹלָה לְכַוֵּין אוֹתָהּ שָׁעָה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Builds on step 9. Now that the moment is defined, the ברייתא says who alone could identify it.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Only בלעם could pinpoint the moment of God's anger, as shown by 'ויודע דעת עליון'.

steps.title: How could בלעם know God's mind if he did not even understand his donkey?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges the reading of 'ויודע דעת עליון'. בלעם could not even understand his own donkey, so how could he know the mind of God?
steps.simpleTranslation: Now, he did not know the mind of his own animal, and he did know the mind of the Most High?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא attacks the idea from Step 10 that בלעם 'knew the knowledge of the Most High.'
steps.deeperAnalysis: In the story of בלעם's donkey, the donkey saw the מלאך and בלעם did not, and בלעם did not understand why it acted as it did. If he could not even understand an animal, it makes no sense that he understood God's thoughts. So 'ויודע דעת עליון' cannot mean real knowledge of God's mind.

keyTerms.meaning: Now (opens a 'how can that be?' challenge)
The mind of his animal (בלעם's donkey)
The mind or knowledge of the Most High (God)

phrases.aramaic: הַשְׁתָּא דַּעַת בְּהֶמְתּוֹ לֹא הֲוָה יָדַע,
phrases.english: Now, the mind of his own animal he did not know,
phrases.notes: Refers to the story of בלעם's donkey in במדבר כב.

phrases.english: and the mind of the Most High he did know?!
phrases.notes: A rhetorical question meaning 'that cannot be.'

steps.triggerLanguage: הַשְׁתָּא דַּעַת בְּהֶמְתּוֹ לֹא הֲוָה יָדַע
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the literal meaning of the פסוק quoted in Step 10.
steps.kashyaTarget: The reading of 'ויודע דעת עליון' as real knowledge of God's mind.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: קל וחומר style logic: someone who could not understand a lower being (his donkey) surely could not understand the highest being (God).

steps.title: בלעם only knew how to time the moment of God's anger
steps.stepSummary: The פסוק does not mean בלעם understood God's thoughts. It means he could pinpoint the exact moment when God is angry.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, the פסוק teaches that he knew how to aim for that exact moment when the הקדוש ברוך הוא is angry.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the challenge by narrowing what בלעם 'knew.'
steps.deeperAnalysis: בלעם did not have deep insight into God's will. He had one narrow skill: timing. He could find the tiny רגע of God's anger described in Step 9 and aim his curse at that moment so it would take effect.

keyTerms.meaning: To aim at, to pinpoint exactly

steps.whyThisMatters: This ties back to Step 9. God's anger lasts only a רגע, so the danger of בלעם was his ability to hit that tiny moment.

phrases.english: Rather, it teaches that he knew
how to pinpoint that moment
in which the Holy One, Blessed be He, is angry.
phrases.notes: At that moment he would say his curse.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Resolves the קשיא of Step 11 by reinterpreting the פסוק.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Reinterpretation: narrows the meaning of 'knowing דעת עליון'.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The פסוק means בלעם understood God's mind.
steps.terutzMaskana: The פסוק means only that בלעם knew how to time the moment of God's anger.

steps.title: A פסוק in מיכה that fits this idea
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא brings the נביא's words to Israel about what בלק plotted, as a source that fits the idea of בלעם and God's anger.
steps.simpleTranslation: And this is what the נביא said to Israel: 'My nation, remember what בלק king of מואב plotted, and so on.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא is setting up a support from a פסוק in מיכה. The support becomes clear only in the next two steps.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The word 'והיינו' means 'and this is what is meant by.' It signals that the idea about בלעם's timing explains this פסוק. The key words come at the end of the פסוק, 'למען דעת צדקות ה׳'. The גמרא will ask about those words next.

keyTerms.meaning: And this is what is meant by (links an idea to a source)
And so on (the rest of the פסוק)

phrases.english: And this is what the prophet said to Israel:
phrases.notes: מיכה ו:ה

phrases.english: "My nation, please remember

phrases.aramaic: מַה יָּעַץ בָּלָק מֶלֶךְ מוֹאָב וְגוֹ׳״.
phrases.english: what Balak king of Moab plotted, etc."
phrases.notes: The פסוק continues: 'and what בלעם answered him... so that you may know the righteous acts of ה׳.'

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Brings a פסוק that will support the idea in Step 12.
steps.raayaObject: That God's anger has a moment which בלעם could have used against Israel.
steps.raayaSupportSource: מיכה ו:ה, 'עמי זכר נא מה יעץ בלק'.

steps.title: What does 'so that you may know the righteous acts of ה׳' mean?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks what the end of the פסוק means. What 'righteous acts' of God are connected to בלק and בלעם?
steps.simpleTranslation: What is meant by 'so that you may know the righteous acts of ה׳'?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks a clarifying question about the last words of the פסוק. The answer will complete the support begun in Step 13.
steps.deeperAnalysis: It is not obvious why remembering בלק's plot should teach us about God's 'צדקות'. The question focuses attention on these words. The answer will show they connect to God's anger.

phrases.english: What is meant by "so that you may know the righteous acts of the Lord"?
phrases.notes: The end of the same פסוק in מיכה.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Zooms in on the key phrase of the פסוק just quoted.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: What 'righteous acts' of God the פסוק refers to in the context of בלעם.

steps.title: God's kindness was not becoming angry during בלעם's days
steps.stepSummary: רבי אלעזר explains that God's 'righteous act' was holding back His anger the whole time בלעם was active, so that בלעם's curse would not work.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי אלעזר said: The הקדוש ברוך הוא said to Israel, 'Know how many kindnesses I did for you, that I did not become angry in the days of בלעם הרשע. For had I become angry, no remnant or survivor would have been left of the enemies of Israel.'
steps.whatsHappening: רבי אלעזר answers the question. The 'צדקות' were that God did not get angry at all while בלעם was trying to curse Israel.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Since בלעם could find the moment of God's anger, any angry moment would have let his curse destroy Israel. So God held back even His daily רגע of anger during those days, and בלעם had no moment to use. This completes the support for Step 12.

keyTerms.meaning: An אמורא who explains the פסוק
For if, had it been that
Literally 'the enemies of Israel', a polite way of saying Israel itself

steps.whatToRemember: בלעם's only power was timing: he could find the רגע of God's anger. God's great kindness was not becoming angry at all during בלעם's days, so his curses failed.
steps.confusionAlert: 'Enemies of Israel' here does NOT mean Israel's actual enemies. It is a polite way of referring to Israel itself, to avoid saying something bad directly about Israel.
steps.whyThisMatters: This shows the פסוק in מיכה really does assume that God has a moment of anger and that בלעם could exploit it. That supports the whole chain from Steps 8 to 12.

phrases.english: Rabbi Elazar said:

phrases.aramaic: אָמַר לָהֶם הַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא לְיִשְׂרָאֵל:
phrases.english: The Holy One, Blessed be He, said to Israel:
Know how many kindnesses I did for you,
phrases.notes: Explains 'דעת צדקות' in the פסוק.

phrases.english: that I did not become angry in the days of Balaam the wicked,
for had I become angry,
there would not have remained of the 'enemies of Israel'
phrases.notes: A polite way of saying 'of Israel.'

phrases.english: a remnant or survivor.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַבִּי אֶלְעָזָר, אָמַר לָהֶם הַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא לְיִשְׂרָאֵל
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the שאלה of Step 14 and completes the support from מיכה.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The 'righteous acts' were that God held back His anger during בלעם's days, so בלעם's curse had no moment in which to take effect.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: God has a brief moment of anger, בלעם knew how to time it, and God kindly withheld it to protect Israel.

steps.title: בלעם admits God was not angry
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא supports רבי אלעזר from בלעם's own words to בלק: 'How can I curse whom God has not cursed?' This shows that God was not angry during all those days.
steps.simpleTranslation: And this is what בלעם said to בלק: 'How can I curse when God has not cursed, and how can I be angry when God has not been angry?' This teaches that during all those days, God was not angry.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a פסוק to back up רבי אלעזר's claim that God held back His anger the whole time בלעם was active.
steps.deeperAnalysis: בלעם's power was to curse at the exact moment of God's anger. Here בלעם himself complains that he cannot curse, because God simply did not get angry. His own words prove that God's 'righteous act' was holding back His anger.

keyTerms.meaning: And this is what (it fits with)

steps.whyThisMatters: It ties together the whole idea: בלעם needed God's anger to make his curse work, and God made sure there was no anger to use.

phrases.english: And this is what Bilam said to Balak:
"How can I curse whom God has not cursed,
phrases.notes: Numbers 23:8

phrases.english: and how can I condemn whom ה׳ has not condemned?"

phrases.aramaic: מְלַמֵּד שֶׁכָּל אוֹתָן הַיָּמִים לֹא זָעַם.
phrases.english: This teaches that all those days, He was not angry.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Supports רבי אלעזר's explanation in step 15 with a פסוק.
steps.raayaObject: That God did not become angry at all during the days of בלעם.
steps.raayaSupportSource: Numbers 23:8, בלעם's words to בלק: 'מה אקב לא קבה אל ומה אזעם לא זעם ה׳'.

steps.title: How long does God's anger last?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks how long God's anger lasts.
steps.simpleTranslation: And how long is His anger?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא is setting up the next move. It asks a clarifying question: how long does God's anger normally last?
steps.deeperAnalysis: This is not a new question. The גמרא repeats the question and answer the ברייתא already gave in step 9 ('וכמה זעמו — רגע'). It does this to bring an אמורא's different definition of a רגע in steps 19–20.

phrases.english: And how long is His anger?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Returns to the ברייתא's question from step 9 about the length of God's anger, in order to give a new definition of רגע.

steps.title: God's anger lasts only a moment
steps.stepSummary: The answer is that God's anger lasts one רגע, a single moment.
steps.simpleTranslation: A moment.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that God's anger lasts only one moment (רגע).
steps.deeperAnalysis: God's anger is extremely short. That is why בלעם needed such an exact skill: he had to catch one tiny moment.

phrases.english: A moment.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question in step 17.

steps.title: How long is a moment?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks for the exact length of a רגע.
steps.simpleTranslation: And how long is a moment?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא is setting up the next move by asking for a precise measure of a רגע.
steps.deeperAnalysis: 'A moment' is vague, so the גמרא wants to know exactly how short it is.

phrases.english: And how long is a moment?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks for a definition of the term given in step 18.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: The exact length of a רגע.

steps.title: A moment is as long as saying the word
steps.stepSummary: רבי אבין (some say רבי אבינא) says a רגע lasts as long as it takes to say the word 'רגע'.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי אבין, and some say רבי אבינא, said: a moment is as long as it takes to say it.
steps.whatsHappening: An אמורא gives the exact length of a רגע: the time it takes to say the word 'רֶגַע'.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This is a different measure from the one in the ברייתא in step 9, which said a רגע is 1/58,888 of an hour. רבי אבין instead defines a רגע as the time it takes to say the word itself. Either way, God's anger lasts only a split second.

keyTerms.meaning: And some say (the statement is from another name)

steps.confusionAlert: 'וְאִיתֵּימָא' does not mean two rabbis argue. It just means there is doubt about which rabbi said this one statement.

phrases.aramaic: אָמַר רַבִּי אָבִין וְאִיתֵּימָא רַבִּי אֲבִינָא:
phrases.english: Rabbi Avin said, and some say Rabbi Avina:
A moment is as long as it takes to say it.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַבִּי אָבִין וְאִיתֵּימָא רַבִּי אֲבִינָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question in step 19.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: A רגע is the time it takes to say the word 'רגע'.

steps.title: What is the source that God is angry for only a moment?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks for a source that God's anger lasts only a moment.
steps.simpleTranslation: And from where do we know that He is angry for a moment?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא is setting up the next move. It asks for a פסוק that proves God's anger lasts only a moment.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Step 18 stated the rule with no source. Now the גמרא wants a פסוק to back it up.

keyTerms.meaning: And from where do we know?

phrases.english: And from where do we know that He is angry for a moment?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks for a source for the answer in step 18.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: A פסוק that proves God's anger lasts only a moment.

steps.title: First proof from תהלים
steps.stepSummary: The proof is the פסוק 'כי רגע באפו חיים ברצונו': His anger lasts a moment, His favor a lifetime.
steps.simpleTranslation: As it says: 'For His anger is for a moment, life is in His favor.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a פסוק from תהלים that says outright that God's anger is for a moment.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The פסוק uses the very word 'רגע' together with 'באפו' (in His anger). It also contrasts this with God's favor, which lasts a whole lifetime.

keyTerms.meaning: As it is said (in a פסוק)

phrases.english: As it is said: "For His anger is for a moment,
phrases.notes: Psalms 30:6

phrases.english: life is in His favor."

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the request for a source in step 21.
steps.raayaObject: That God's anger lasts only a moment.

steps.title: Second proof from ישעיה
steps.stepSummary: A second source: 'חבי כמעט רגע עד יעבר זעם': hide for a brief moment until the anger passes.
steps.simpleTranslation: And if you want, say it from here: 'Hide for a brief moment, until the anger passes.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא offers a second פסוק, from ישעיה, that also shows God's anger lasts only a moment.
steps.deeperAnalysis: 'ואי בעית אימא' brings another option for a source, not a disagreement. The פסוק says you only need to hide for a moment, because by then the anger has already passed.

keyTerms.meaning: And if you want, say (another option)

steps.whatToRemember: God's anger lasts only one רגע, the time it takes to say the word. Two פסוקים prove it: 'כי רגע באפו' and 'חבי כמעט רגע עד יעבר זעם'.

phrases.english: And if you wish, say it from here:
"Hide for a brief moment,
phrases.notes: Isaiah 26:20

phrases.english: until the anger passes."

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives an alternative source for the same point as step 22.
steps.raayaObject: That God's anger lasts only a moment.

steps.title: When does God get angry?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks at what time God's moment of anger happens.
steps.simpleTranslation: And when is He angry?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא is setting up the next move. It asks when during the day God's moment of anger happens.
steps.deeperAnalysis: We now know how long the anger lasts. The next question is when it occurs, since that is exactly the moment בלעם knew how to find.

phrases.english: And when is He angry?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves from how long the anger lasts to when it happens.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: The time of day when God's moment of anger happens.

steps.title: אביי: in the first three hours, with a sign from the rooster
steps.stepSummary: אביי says the anger comes during the first three hours of the day. You can tell by the rooster: its comb turns white and it stands on one leg.
steps.simpleTranslation: אביי said: during those first three hours of the day, when the rooster's comb turns white and it stands on one leg.
steps.whatsHappening: אביי answers that God's anger comes within the first three hours of the day, and he gives a sign in nature to recognize it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: אביי gives a time range, the first three hours, and a sign for the exact moment. At that moment the rooster's red comb goes white and it stands on one leg. The next step challenges whether this sign really shows anything.

keyTerms.meaning: The first three hours (of the day)

steps.confusionAlert: The rooster does not cause the anger. It is only a sign that shows when the moment of anger is happening.

phrases.english: Abaye said:
During those first three hours (of the day),
when the comb of the rooster turns white
and it stands on one leg.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר אַבַּיֵי: בְּהָנָךְ תְּלָת שָׁעֵי קַמָּיָיתָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question in step 24.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: During the first three hours of the day, at the moment the rooster's comb turns white and it stands on one leg.

steps.title: But the rooster always stands that way
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges אביי's sign: a rooster stands on one leg at all hours, so how can that show anything?
steps.simpleTranslation: But doesn't the rooster stand like this every single hour?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא pokes a hole in אביי's sign. Roosters stand on one leg all the time, so standing on one leg can't point to one special moment.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A sign is only useful if it shows up at one particular time. If roosters stand this way constantly, the sign doesn't single out the moment of anger. The question is worded as a question, but it really works as a challenge to the sign.

phrases.english: Every single hour
does it not also stand like this?
phrases.notes: Refers to the rooster standing on one leg.

steps.triggerLanguage: כֹּל שַׁעְתָּא וְשַׁעְתָּא נָמֵי קָאֵי הָכִי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the sign that אביי gave in step 25.
steps.kashyaTarget: אביי's sign that the rooster stands on one leg during the moment of anger.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: A sign that appears all the time cannot identify one specific moment.

steps.title: The red streaks are the real sign
steps.stepSummary: Normally the rooster's comb has red streaks. During the moment of anger, the red streaks are gone.
steps.simpleTranslation: At every other hour, there are red streaks in its comb. At that hour, there are no red streaks in it.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the challenge. The real difference is in the comb: usually it has red streaks, but at the moment of anger it has none, so it looks fully white.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Standing on one leg alone proves nothing. The sign only works together with the comb losing all its red streaks. This explains אביי's words from step 25, that the comb turns white.

phrases.english: Every other hour
there are red streaks in it (its comb)
but at that hour (the moment of anger)
there are no red streaks in it

steps.whatToRemember: The sign of God's moment of anger is a rooster standing on one leg whose comb has no red streaks at all.
steps.triggerLanguage: כֹּל שַׁעְתָּא אִית בֵּיהּ שׁוּרְיָיקֵי סוּמָּקֵי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of step 26.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Clarifies which detail of the sign actually matters.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The sign seemed useless, because roosters stand on one leg all the time.
steps.terutzMaskana: The sign is the comb with no red streaks, which happens only at the moment of anger.

steps.title: רבי יהושע בן לוי plans to curse a heretic
steps.stepSummary: A heretic kept bothering רבי יהושע בן לוי with challenges about פסוקים. So he set up a rooster to find the moment of anger and planned to curse him then.
steps.simpleTranslation: There was a certain heretic in רבי יהושע בן לוי's neighborhood who bothered him a lot about פסוקים. One day he took a rooster, placed it between the legs of his bed, and watched it. He thought: when that moment comes, I will curse him.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא begins a story that puts the rooster sign into practice. This step sets up the scene and the plan. The outcome comes in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי יהושע בן לוי wanted to use the moment of God's anger as a weapon, since a curse at that time would take effect. The story will test whether doing this is proper.

phrases.english: A certain heretic

phrases.aramaic: דַּהֲוָה בְּשִׁבְבוּתֵיהּ דְּרַבִּי יְהוֹשֻׁעַ בֶּן לֵוִי,
phrases.english: who lived in the neighborhood of Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi

phrases.aramaic: הֲוָה קָא מְצַעֵר לֵיהּ טוּבָא בִּקְרָאֵי.
phrases.english: would bother him a lot about verses
phrases.notes: He kept challenging the meaning of פסוקים.

phrases.english: One day he took a rooster
and placed it between the legs of the bed
and watched it

phrases.aramaic: סְבַר: כִּי מָטָא הַהִיא שַׁעְתָּא, אֶלְטְיֵיהּ.
phrases.english: He thought: When that moment arrives, I will curse him.

steps.triggerLanguage: הַהוּא מִינָא דַּהֲוָה בְּשִׁבְבוּתֵיהּ דְּרַבִּי יְהוֹשֻׁעַ בֶּן לֵוִי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Tells a story that uses the rooster sign just explained.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Sets up the story: רבי יהושע בן לוי plans to curse the heretic at the moment of God's anger.

steps.title: He fell asleep and learned not to curse
steps.stepSummary: At the exact moment, רבי יהושע בן לוי fell asleep. He concluded that cursing people is improper, since God's mercy is on all His creations.
steps.simpleTranslation: When that moment arrived, he fell asleep. He said: Learn from this that it is not proper to do this. It is written: 'His mercy is on all His works.'
steps.whatsHappening: The plan fails because he dozes off at exactly the right moment. He takes this as a message from Heaven that he should not have tried it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Falling asleep at that exact time was not an accident. It showed that cursing is not proper conduct (אורח ארעא), even against a wicked person. He backs this up with a פסוק: God's mercy covers everyone, including sinners.

keyTerms.meaning: His mercy is on all His works (תהלים קמ״ה)

phrases.english: When that moment arrived, he fell asleep.
He said: Learn from this
that it is not proper conduct to do this
"His mercy is on all His works" is written.

steps.whatToRemember: Even though there is a moment when a curse could work, it is wrong to use it. God's mercy reaches everyone.
steps.whyThisMatters: The story turns a piece of information (when God's anger happens) into a lesson in character: we should not try to bring harm on others.
steps.triggerLanguage: אֲמַר: שְׁמַע מִינַּהּ, לָאו אוֹרַח אַרְעָא לְמֶעְבַּד הָכִי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives the outcome of the plan from step 28 and the lesson drawn from it.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: It is not proper to curse people, even wicked ones, because God's mercy is on all His creations.

steps.title: A second verse: punishing is not good
steps.stepSummary: A second פסוק supports the lesson: even causing punishment to come upon someone is not good.
steps.simpleTranslation: And it is written: 'Punishment, even for the righteous, is not good.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא adds another פסוק to strengthen רבי יהושע בן לוי's conclusion. Bringing punishment onto someone is not the right thing to do.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The first פסוק focused on God's mercy toward the sinner. This פסוק looks at the person who causes the punishment: even for a צדיק, bringing punishment on another person is 'not good.' Together, the two פסוקים show the lesson from both sides.

keyTerms.meaning: And it is written (introduces another פסוק)

phrases.english: And it is written: "Punishment, even for the righteous, is not good."
phrases.notes: משלי י״ז:כ״ו. Read here as: even a righteous person should not bring punishment on others.

steps.confusionAlert: In this context the פסוק does not mean that a righteous person should never be punished. It is read to mean that it is not good for a righteous person to cause punishment to someone else.
steps.triggerLanguage: וּכְתִיב: גַּם עָנוֹשׁ לַצַּדִּיק לֹא טוֹב
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Adds a second source for the conclusion of step 29.
steps.raayaObject: The lesson that one should not curse or bring punishment on others.
steps.raayaSupportSource: משלי י״ז:כ״ו — גם ענוש לצדיק לא טוב

steps.title: Why God grows angry each morning
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא in the name of רבי מאיר explains that God's daily anger comes when the kings bow to the sun at sunrise.
steps.simpleTranslation: It was taught in the name of רבי מאיר: when the sun rises, all the kings of the East and West put their crowns on their heads and bow to the sun. Right away, הקדוש ברוך הוא becomes angry.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a ברייתא that explains what causes the daily moment of God's anger it has been discussing.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Earlier the גמרא said there is a short moment of anger every day. Now we learn the reason: people treat the sun as a god by bowing to it at sunrise. Because this happens every morning, the anger also comes every morning.

keyTerms.meaning: It was taught, introducing a ברייתא

steps.whyThisMatters: It gives a reason for the daily moment of anger, so the whole earlier discussion about that moment now makes sense.

phrases.english: It was taught in the name of Rabbi Meir:
At the time when the sun rises,
and all the kings of the East and the West
place their crowns on their heads
and bow down to the sun,
immediately the Holy One, Blessed be He, grows angry.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Explains the cause of the daily moment of anger discussed in the earlier steps.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: God's daily anger is triggered when the kings bow to the sun at sunrise.

steps.title: One moment of inner regret beats many lashes
steps.stepSummary: רבי יוחנן, quoting רבי יוסי, teaches that one honest pang of regret in a person's heart is better than many lashes. He proves it from a פסוק in הושע.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי יוחנן said in the name of רבי יוסי: one moment of regret in a person's heart is better than many lashes. As it says: 'She will chase her lovers, and so on, and she will say, I will go back to my first husband, because it was better for me then than now.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a new teaching in the same chain of sayings from רבי יוחנן in the name of רבי יוסי. This one is about the power of inner regret.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In the פסוק, ישראל is compared to a wife who strays and then decides on her own to return. A feeling of regret from inside changes a person more than punishment from outside. That is why the many punishments listed in the following פסוקים are worth less than this one moment of returning.

keyTerms.meaning: Inner regret or self-correction, a pang of conscience
My first husband (a picture of God)

steps.confusionAlert: Here מַרְדּוּת does not mean rebellion. It means a person correcting himself through regret in his own heart.

phrases.aramaic: וְאָמַר רַבִּי יוֹחָנָן מִשּׁוּם רַבִּי יוֹסֵי:
phrases.english: And Rabbi Yochanan said in the name of Rabbi Yosei:

phrases.aramaic: טוֹבָה מַרְדּוּת אַחַת בְּלִבּוֹ שֶׁל אָדָם
phrases.english: One pang of regret in a person's heart is better
than many lashes.
As it is stated: "And she will chase her lovers, etc.,
and she will say: I will go and return
to my first husband,
for it was better for me then than now."

steps.triggerLanguage: וְאָמַר רַבִּי יוֹחָנָן מִשּׁוּם רַבִּי יוֹסֵי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: A new teaching in the series of sayings from רבי יוחנן in the name of רבי יוסי.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: One moment of inner regret is better than many lashes.

steps.title: ריש לקיש: better than a hundred lashes
steps.stepSummary: ריש לקיש makes the same point with an exact number: inner regret is better than a hundred lashes. He brings a פסוק from משלי.
steps.simpleTranslation: ריש לקיש said: it is better than a hundred lashes. As it says: 'A rebuke goes deeper into a person who understands than a hundred blows into a fool.'
steps.whatsHappening: ריש לקיש adds his own version of the teaching. He uses a different פסוק that gives the number one hundred.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי יוחנן said 'many lashes', and ריש לקיש says 'a hundred lashes'. His פסוק teaches that a wise person learns more from one rebuke than a fool learns from a hundred hits. The idea is the same, but he gives a stronger and more exact measure.

keyTerms.meaning: An אמורא, the study partner of רבי יוחנן

steps.whatToRemember: Inner change is stronger than outside punishment. רבי יוחנן says it beats many lashes, and ריש לקיש says it beats a hundred.

phrases.english: And Reish Lakish said:
more than one hundred lashes,
as it is stated: "A rebuke enters deeper into a man of understanding
than striking a fool a hundred times."

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives a parallel version of רבי יוחנן's teaching with a more exact number and a different פסוק.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Inner regret is better than one hundred lashes.

steps.title: משה's first request: the שכינה rests on ישראל
steps.stepSummary: רבי יוחנן, quoting רבי יוסי, says משה asked God for three things and received all of them. The first was that the שכינה rest on ישראל.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי יוחנן said in the name of רבי יוסי: משה asked הקדוש ברוך הוא for three things, and God gave them to him. He asked that the שכינה rest on ישראל, and God gave it to him, as it says: 'Is it not in that You go with us?'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings another teaching from the same chain, a list of three requests משה made. This step gives the opening line and the first request.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The words 'Is it not in that You go with us' are משה asking that God's presence stay with the Jewish people. The phrase 'וְנָתַן לוֹ' tells us God agreed. The other requests follow in the next steps.

keyTerms.meaning: And He gave it to him (the request was granted)

phrases.aramaic: וְאָמַר רַבִּי יוֹחָנָן מִשּׁוּם רַבִּי יוֹסֵי:
phrases.english: And Rabbi Yochanan said in the name of Rabbi Yosei:
Moses requested three things

phrases.aramaic: מִלִּפְנֵי הַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא, וְנָתַן לוֹ.
phrases.english: from before the Holy One, Blessed be He, and He granted them to him.
He requested that the Divine Presence rest upon Israel,
and He granted it to him, as it is stated:
"Is it not in that You go with us?"

steps.triggerLanguage: וְאָמַר רַבִּי יוֹחָנָן מִשּׁוּם רַבִּי יוֹסֵי: שְׁלֹשָׁה דְּבָרִים בִּקֵּשׁ מֹשֶׁה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: A new teaching in the same series of sayings from רבי יוחנן in the name of רבי יוסי.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: משה asked for three things and all were granted. The first was that the שכינה rest on ישראל.

steps.title: משה's second request: no שכינה on the nations
steps.stepSummary: The second request was that the שכינה not rest on the nations of the world, and God granted it. The proof is 'We will be set apart, I and Your people.'
steps.simpleTranslation: He asked that the שכינה not rest on the nations who serve stars and idols, and God gave it to him, as it says: 'And we will be set apart, I and Your people.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא continues the list with the second of משה's three requests.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The first request was for God's presence to rest on ישראל. The second asks that this presence be special to ישראל and not rest on the other nations. The word 'וְנִפְלִינוּ' means 'we will be set apart', which shows ישראל has a unique closeness to God.

keyTerms.meaning: Idol worshippers, literally 'those who serve the stars' (the nations)
And we will be set apart, distinguished

phrases.english: He requested that the Divine Presence not rest
upon the idol worshippers (the nations),
and He granted it to him, as it is stated:
"So that we are set apart, I and Your people."

steps.triggerLanguage: בִּקֵּשׁ שֶׁלֹּא תִּשְׁרֶה שְׁכִינָה עַל עוֹבְדֵי כּוֹכָבִים
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the list of משה's three requests with the second one.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: משה's second request was that the שכינה not rest on the nations, and it was granted.

steps.title: משה's third request: to know God's ways
steps.stepSummary: The third request of משה was to understand how the הקדוש ברוך הוא runs the world. It was granted, and the גמרא proves it from a פסוק.
steps.simpleTranslation: משה asked that the ways of the Holy One, Blessed be He, be made known to him, and God granted it. As it says: 'Please make known to me Your ways.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives the third and last of משה's three requests: to understand God's ways. It shows from a פסוק that משה asked for this.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This completes the list that began in steps 34 and 35. The first two requests were about where the שכינה rests. This request is different: it is about understanding how God treats people. It also sets up the question that comes next.

keyTerms.meaning: His ways (how God runs the world)

phrases.aramaic: בִּקֵּשׁ לְהוֹדִיעוֹ דְּרָכָיו שֶׁל הַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא,
phrases.english: He requested that the ways of the Holy One, Blessed be He, be made known to him,
and He granted it to him,
as it is said: 'Please make known to me Your ways.'
phrases.notes: שמות לג:יג

steps.triggerLanguage: בִּקֵּשׁ לְהוֹדִיעוֹ דְּרָכָיו שֶׁל הַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Third item in the list of משה's three requests
steps.mimraCoreRuling: משה asked to understand God's ways, and this request was granted.

steps.title: Why do good and bad people have good or bad lives?
steps.stepSummary: משה asks God to explain the four combinations: a צדיק who does well, a צדיק who suffers, a רשע who does well, and a רשע who suffers.
steps.simpleTranslation: משה said before Him: Master of the World! Why is there a צדיק who has good, and a צדיק who has bad? Why is there a רשע who has good, and a רשע who has bad?
steps.whatsHappening: Now we learn what 'knowing God's ways' meant. משה asks the classic question of why good people suffer and bad people do well.
steps.deeperAnalysis: משה lists all four possibilities, not only the two puzzling ones. That way, whatever answer God gives has to explain every case. The answer comes in the next step.

keyTerms.meaning: a righteous person who has a good life
a wicked person who has a bad life

phrases.english: He said before Him: Master of the World!

phrases.aramaic: מִפְּנֵי מָה יֵשׁ צַדִּיק וְטוֹב לוֹ,
phrases.english: Why is there a righteous person who has good,
and there is a righteous person who has bad,
there is a wicked person who has good,
and there is a wicked person who has bad?

steps.triggerLanguage: מִפְּנֵי מָה יֵשׁ צַדִּיק וְטוֹב לוֹ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Spells out what משה wanted to know about God's ways
steps.sheelahInformationSought: The reason behind the four combinations of righteousness and fortune

steps.title: God's answer: it depends on the parents
steps.stepSummary: God answers that a person's fortune depends on whether his father was a צדיק or a רשע.
steps.simpleTranslation: God said to him: משה, a צדיק who has good is a צדיק son of a צדיק. A צדיק who has bad is a צדיק son of a רשע. A רשע who has good is a רשע son of a צדיק. A רשע who has bad is a רשע son of a רשע.
steps.whatsHappening: God answers משה. A good or bad life comes from the father's deeds: a righteous father brings good, and a wicked father brings bad.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Each person's life is explained by two things: his own deeds and his father's deeds. The father's merit or sin decides whether he does well or suffers. The גמרא will challenge this explanation in the next step.

keyTerms.meaning: a righteous person, son of a righteous person
a righteous person, son of a wicked person
a wicked person, son of a righteous person

phrases.english: He said to him: Moshe,

phrases.aramaic: צַדִּיק וְטוֹב לוֹ — צַדִּיק בֶּן צַדִּיק.
phrases.english: a righteous person who has good is a righteous person, son of a righteous person.

phrases.aramaic: צַדִּיק וְרַע לוֹ — צַדִּיק בֶּן רָשָׁע.
phrases.english: A righteous person who has bad is a righteous person, son of a wicked person.

phrases.aramaic: רָשָׁע וְטוֹב לוֹ — רָשָׁע בֶּן צַדִּיק.
phrases.english: A wicked person who has good is a wicked person, son of a righteous person.

phrases.aramaic: רָשָׁע וְרַע לוֹ — רָשָׁע בֶּן רָשָׁע.
phrases.english: A wicked person who has bad is a wicked person, son of a wicked person.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers משה's question
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: Fortune depends on the father's righteousness or wickedness.

steps.title: Challenge: are children really punished for their fathers?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes the answer again and questions it. It points to two פסוקים that seem to contradict each other about punishing children for their fathers' sins.
steps.simpleTranslation: The master said: a צדיק who has good is a צדיק son of a צדיק, and a צדיק who has bad is a צדיק son of a רשע. Is that so? But it is written, 'He visits the sin of fathers upon children,' and it is written, 'Children shall not be put to death for fathers.' And we pointed out that these פסוקים contradict each other.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא repeats the answer about a צדיק son of a רשע and asks, 'Is that really true?' It then sets up the attack by recalling two פסוקים that seem to contradict each other.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The target is the idea that a righteous son suffers because of his wicked father. The גמרא brings in a well-known contradiction between two פסוקים: one says children are punished for fathers, and the other says they are not. The way that contradiction was resolved will be used against the answer in the next step.

keyTerms.meaning: The master said (quoting an earlier statement to discuss it)
He visits the sin of fathers upon children
and we pointed out that the פסוקים contradict each other

phrases.english: The master said:

phrases.aramaic: צַדִּיק וְטוֹב לוֹ — צַדִּיק בֶּן צַדִּיק,
phrases.english: a righteous person who has good is a righteous person, son of a righteous person;

phrases.aramaic: צַדִּיק וְרַע לוֹ — צַדִּיק בֶּן רָשָׁע.
phrases.english: a righteous person who has bad is a righteous person, son of a wicked person.
Is that so?

phrases.aramaic: וְהָא כְּתִיב: ״פֹּקֵד עֲוֹן אָבוֹת עַל בָּנִים״,
phrases.english: But it is written: 'He visits the sin of fathers upon children,'
phrases.notes: שמות לד:ז

phrases.english: and it is written: 'And children shall not be put to death for fathers,'
phrases.notes: דברים כד:טז

phrases.english: and we raised a contradiction between these verses,

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Repeats the answer from step 38 in order to challenge it
steps.kashyaTarget: The claim that a righteous son suffers because of a wicked father
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Two פסוקים about punishing children for fathers' sins, and how they were reconciled, will show that a צדיק is not punished for his father.

steps.title: The known resolution: only if they keep their fathers' ways
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא recalls how the two פסוקים were reconciled. Children are punished only if they continue their fathers' sins. This completes the challenge, because a צדיק does not continue his father's sins.
steps.simpleTranslation: And we resolved it: it is not difficult. This פסוק is when they hold on to their fathers' deeds. That פסוק is when they do not hold on to their fathers' deeds.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא recalls the accepted answer to the contradiction. Children suffer for their fathers only when they keep doing the same sins. This answer finishes the attack on God's reply to משה.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A צדיק, by definition, does not continue his wicked father's deeds. So by this rule he should not be punished for them. That means 'a צדיק son of a רשע' cannot explain why a צדיק suffers.

keyTerms.meaning: they hold on to their fathers' deeds (they continue the same sins)

steps.confusionAlert: The words 'לא קשיא' here do NOT answer the challenge against God's reply to משה. They are a recalled answer to the older contradiction between the two פסוקים. That recalled answer is actually what makes the challenge work.

phrases.english: And we resolved it: it is not difficult.
This verse is when they hold on to their fathers' deeds,

phrases.aramaic: הָא — כְּשֶׁאֵין אוֹחֲזִין מַעֲשֵׂה אֲבוֹתֵיהֶם בִּידֵיהֶם.
phrases.english: and that verse is when they do not hold on to their fathers' deeds.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Completes the challenge begun in step 39
steps.kashyaTarget: 'A צדיק who suffers is the son of a רשע'
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Children are punished only if they continue their fathers' sins. A צדיק does not, so he cannot be suffering because of his father.

steps.title: New reading: complete versus partial righteousness
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא reinterprets God's answer. Fortune depends on whether a person is a complete צדיק or רשע, or only a partial one.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, this is what He said to him: a צדיק who has good is a complete צדיק. A צדיק who has bad is an incomplete צדיק. A רשע who has good is an incomplete רשע. A רשע who has bad is a complete רשע.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא drops the 'father' explanation. It says God really meant that it depends on whether the person is completely good or bad, or only partly.
steps.deeperAnalysis: An incomplete צדיק has some sins, so he is punished for them in this world and receives full reward in עולם הבא. An incomplete רשע has some good deeds, so he is rewarded for them in this world and receives full punishment later. The complete צדיק and the complete רשע get only good or only bad.

keyTerms.meaning: this is what He said to him

steps.whatToRemember: Our conclusion: a צדיק who suffers is not being punished for his father. He is an incomplete צדיק, paying for his few sins in this world. A רשע who does well is an incomplete רשע, being rewarded here for his few good deeds.
steps.whyThisMatters: This becomes a basic principle in Jewish thought about why good people suffer. Suffering in this world can be how a person pays for his sins before receiving his reward in עולם הבא.

phrases.english: Rather, this is what He said to him:
a righteous person who has good is a completely righteous person;

phrases.aramaic: צַדִּיק וְרַע לוֹ — צַדִּיק שֶׁאֵינוֹ גָּמוּר,
phrases.english: a righteous person who has bad is a righteous person who is not complete;

phrases.aramaic: רָשָׁע וְטוֹב לוֹ — רָשָׁע שֶׁאֵינוֹ גָּמוּר,
phrases.english: a wicked person who has good is a wicked person who is not complete;
a wicked person who has bad is a completely wicked person.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge by reinterpreting God's reply from step 38
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Fortune depends on the father's deeds.
steps.terutzMaskana: Fortune depends on whether the person himself is completely or partially righteous or wicked.

steps.title: רבי מאיר: only two of משה's three requests were granted
steps.stepSummary: רבי מאיר disagrees with רבי יוחנן. Only two of משה's requests were granted. God did not grant the request to understand His ways (why צדיקים suffer and רשעים prosper). The proof is the פסוק saying God grants grace and mercy even to those who are not worthy.
steps.simpleTranslation: This disagrees with רבי מאיר. רבי מאיר said: two requests were given to משה, and one was not. As the פסוק says, "I will be gracious to whom I will be gracious," even if he is not worthy. And "I will have mercy on whom I will have mercy," even if he is not worthy.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא points out that everything we just learned follows רבי יוחנן, who said all three requests were granted. רבי מאיר disagrees and says the third request was refused.
steps.deeperAnalysis: According to רבי יוחנן, God explained His ways to משה. That is why the previous steps discussed the four kinds of צדיק and רשע. רבי מאיר reads the פסוק "וחנותי את אשר אחון" as God saying, "I give grace and mercy as I choose, even to the unworthy." In other words, God would not explain the reasons behind how He treats people.

keyTerms.meaning: And this disagrees with (the opinion of)

steps.confusionAlert: The one who 'disagrees with רבי מאיר' is רבי יוחנן. His statement that משה got all three requests started this discussion earlier. It is not the explanation in step 41.
steps.whyThisMatters: This sets up two basic views: either משה was shown why good and bad things happen to people, or even משה was not shown this.

phrases.english: And this disagrees with Rabbi Meir,
phrases.notes: That is, רבי יוחנן's view that all three requests were granted.

phrases.english: for Rabbi Meir said:
Two (requests) were given to him
phrases.notes: The שכינה rests on Israel, and it does not rest on the nations.

phrases.english: and one was not given to him,
phrases.notes: The request to know God's ways.

phrases.english: as it says: "And I will be gracious to whom I will be gracious"
even though he is not worthy,
"and I will have mercy on whom I will have mercy"
even though he is not worthy.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Shows that the whole discussion of the four combinations assumed רבי יוחנן's view. Then it gives רבי מאיר's opposing view.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Only two of משה's requests were granted. God's ways of giving grace and mercy were not revealed to him.

steps.title: When I wanted, you did not want
steps.stepSummary: On the פסוק "You cannot see My face," רבי יהושע בן קרחה teaches that God told משה: at the burning bush I wanted to show you, and you hid your face. Now that you want to see, I do not want to show you.
steps.simpleTranslation: "And He said: You cannot see My face." It was taught in the name of רבי יהושע בן קרחה: this is what הקדוש ברוך הוא said to משה: When I wanted, you did not want. Now that you want, I do not want.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא moves to a new פסוק in the same story and brings an explanation of why God refused to show משה His face.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי יהושע בן קרחה connects two moments. At the burning bush, משה hid his face. Now משה asks to see God's glory. In this view, hiding his face at the bush was a missed chance, and משה lost something because of it.

keyTerms.meaning: It was taught (a teaching from the תנאים)

phrases.english: "And He said: You cannot see My face,"

phrases.aramaic: תָּנָא מִשְּׁמֵיהּ דְּרַבִּי יְהוֹשֻׁעַ בֶּן קָרְחָה,
phrases.english: it was taught in the name of Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korcha:

phrases.aramaic: כָּךְ אָמַר לוֹ הַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא לְמֹשֶׁה:
phrases.english: So said the Holy One, Blessed be He, to Moshe:
When I wanted (to show you), you did not want (to see),
phrases.notes: At the burning bush: "ויסתר משה פניו".

phrases.english: now that you want, I do not want.

steps.triggerLanguage: וַיֹּאמֶר לֹא תוּכַל לִרְאוֹת אֶת פָּנָי תָּנָא מִשְּׁמֵיהּ דְּרַבִּי יְהוֹשֻׁעַ בֶּן קָרְחָה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves on to the next פסוק in the same conversation between God and משה.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Because משה hid his face at the burning bush, God later refused to show him His face.

steps.title: רבי יונתן: three rewards for three acts
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא notes that רבי יהושע בן קרחה's view disagrees with רבי שמואל בר נחמני in the name of רבי יונתן. That view says משה was rewarded three times for three things he did at the burning bush.
steps.simpleTranslation: This disagrees with what רבי שמואל בר נחמני said in the name of רבי יונתן. For רבי שמואל בר נחמני said in the name of רבי יונתן: as a reward for three things, משה earned three things.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא introduces an opposite view about משה hiding his face. This line is a headline that sets up the list of three rewards in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי יהושע בן קרחה treated hiding his face as a missed chance. רבי יונתן treats it as an act of humility and awe that was rewarded. That is the disagreement.
steps.confusionAlert: Here 'ופליגא' means רבי יונתן disagrees with רבי יהושע בן קרחה from the step just before. It is not about רבי מאיר.

phrases.english: And this disagrees with Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani,
who said in the name of Rabbi Yonatan,
for Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani said
that Rabbi Yonatan said:
As a reward for three (things), he merited three.

steps.triggerLanguage: וּפְלִיגָא דְּרַבִּי שְׁמוּאֵל בַּר נַחְמָנִי אָמַר רַבִּי יוֹנָתָן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Brings an opinion that argues with רבי יהושע בן קרחה.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: משה's three acts of holding back at the burning bush earned him three rewards.

steps.title: The three rewards listed
steps.stepSummary: Each act at the burning bush matches a reward. He hid his face, so his face shone. He was afraid, so others were afraid to come near him. He would not look, so he was allowed to see the image of God.
steps.simpleTranslation: As a reward for "משה hid his face," he earned a glowing face. As a reward for "for he was afraid," he earned "they were afraid to come near him." As a reward for "to look," he earned "he sees the image of ה׳."
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא spells out the three rewards announced in the previous step. Each one matches a word from the burning bush פסוק.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Each part of שמות ג:ו (hiding the face, fear, not looking) is paired with a matching reward. The rewards are the shining face, the people's awe of him, and seeing the image of ה׳. The reward mirrors the act.

steps.whatToRemember: There are two opposite views of משה hiding his face at the bush. רבי יהושע בן קרחה says he lost out: "When I wanted, you didn't." רבי יונתן says he was rewarded three times, measure for measure.

steps.title: משה was shown the knot of God's תפילין
steps.stepSummary: רב חנא בר ביזנא, in the name of רבי שמעון חסידא, explains that 'you will see My back' means God showed משה the קשר של תפילין.
steps.simpleTranslation: The פסוק says: 'I will remove My hand, and you will see My back.' רב חנא בר ביזנא said in the name of רבי שמעון חסידא: This teaches that the Holy One showed משה the knot of the תפילין.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא explains what משה actually saw when God said he would see His 'back.' The answer is the קשר של תפילין, which sits at the back of the head.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The גמרא returns to the conversation in שמות לג, where God said 'You cannot see My face' (step 43) and then 'you will see My back.' The word 'אחורי' (My back) is read as the back of the head, where the knot of the head-תפילין rests. This builds on the teaching on the previous amud (ו.) that God, so to speak, wears תפילין.

keyTerms.meaning: My back — here read as the back of the head
The knot of the תפילין, which rests at the back of the head
'This teaches' — a formula that introduces a lesson drawn from a פסוק

steps.confusionAlert: God has no physical body. The גמרא is using a deep image built on the earlier teaching that God 'wears תפילין.' It is not describing a literal body.

steps.title: God never takes back a promise of good
steps.stepSummary: רבי יוחנן in the name of רבי יוסי teaches that any good promise God makes, even a conditional one, is never taken back.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי יוחנן said in the name of רבי יוסי: Every statement for good that came out of the mouth of the Holy One, even if it was made with a condition, He never took back.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a new teaching about God's promises. When God promises something good, it always comes true in the end.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The new point is the phrase 'even על תנאי (on a condition).' Even if the condition seems to fail, the good promise still gets fulfilled in some way. This sets up the next steps, which will look for a source for this rule.

keyTerms.meaning: For good — a promise of good
He did not take it back

steps.whyThisMatters: It teaches that God's promises of good are permanent. This idea shows up in many places in Jewish thought.

steps.title: Asking for the source of this rule
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks how we know that God never takes back a good promise.
steps.simpleTranslation: From where do we know this?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks for a source for רבי יוסי's rule. This short question sets up the proof in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This is not an attack on the rule. It is a request to show where the rule comes from in the פסוקים.

steps.title: Proof from God's promise to make משה a great nation
steps.stepSummary: God promised to make משה into a mighty nation. משה's prayer cancelled the decree, yet the promise was still fulfilled through his descendants.
steps.simpleTranslation: We know it from משה רבינו. God said: 'Leave Me alone and I will destroy them, and I will make you into a mighty nation.' משה prayed about this and cancelled the decree. Even so, God fulfilled the promise through משה's descendants. As the פסוק says: 'The sons of משה were גרשום and אליעזר. The sons of אליעזר were רחביה the chief. And the sons of רחביה were very many.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא proves רבי יוסי's rule from the story of the golden calf. God's promise to make משה a great nation still came true, even though the plan it was attached to was cancelled.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The promise to make משה great was tied to a condition: that Israel would be destroyed. משה's prayer cancelled that condition, so you might think the promise was cancelled too. But God kept the good part anyway, through רחביה's many descendants.

steps.title: רחביה's descendants were more than 600,000
steps.stepSummary: רב יוסף teaches that 'רבו למעלה' means more than 600,000. He learns this through a גזירה שוה from the word for 'many' used about בני ישראל in Egypt.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב יוסף taught: 'Very many' means more than 600,000. This is learned from the word 'many' appearing in two places. Here it is written: 'They were very many.' And there it is written: 'And בני ישראל were fruitful, swarmed, and became many.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא finishes the proof by showing that רחביה's descendants truly became a 'mighty nation.' It shows their number matched the size of all of Israel.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The word 'many' is used about בני ישראל in מצרים, and they numbered 600,000. Using a גזירה שוה, the same word about רחביה's sons tells us they were also over 600,000. That makes משה's family a nation as big as Israel, so God's promise was truly kept.

keyTerms.meaning: Taught — introduces a teaching from a ברייתא
Sixty times ten thousand, which is 600,000
It is learned from the shared word 'many' — a גזירה שוה
It is written here... and it is written there — the standard way of setting up a גזירה שוה

steps.whatToRemember: God's good promise to משה came true even after the decree was cancelled. רחביה's descendants alone grew to more than 600,000, as large as all of Israel. This proves that a good promise from God is never taken back.
